newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia ruling Lib Dems win most votes in poll.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia ruling Lib Dems win most votes in poll.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats on Sunday won the most votes in the country's second general election since independence from Yugoslavia, according to partial results.

With 42 percent of the vote counted, the National Electoral Commission said the Liberal Democrats had won 27.15 percent of the vote, around four percent more than in the last general election in 1992.

Drnovsek, 46, president of the former Yugoslav federation between 1989 and 1990, had been credited with securing a stable democracy and prosperous economy in Slovenia during his four- year term of office.
"We will be in a position to form a coalition, but the result is tight," the Liberal Democrats' general secretary, Gregor Golobic, told Reuters.
In a sign of a shift to the right in Slovenian politics, rightwing parties increased their share of the overall vote.
Partial results showed the conservative People's Party, led by 36-year-old Marjan Podobnik, with 20.45 percent, and the centre-right Social Democrats third on 15.97 percent.
The Christian Democrats, junior partners in Drnovsek's government, received 10.36 percent of the vote, with the United List of Social Democrats, the former communists, just behind with 8.42 percent.
Drnovsek had faced a loose pre-electoral alliance of rightwing parties, called the "Slovenian Spring", comprising the People's Party, Social Democrats and Christian Democrats.

The three parties had a combined vote of 47.6 percent but it was not immediately clear whether they would present themselves to President Milan Kucan as a viable alternative to Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats.
"According to results so far, we could be the top party in the 'Slovenian Spring' coalition," People's Party deputy leader Janez Podobnik, the brother of leader Marjan, said.
But the Liberal Democrats' Golobic described the "Slovenian Spring" coalition as fragile, hinting that one or two of the rightwing parties may be invited to join a partnership with Drnovsek.

Kucan, Slovenia's former communist party chief who defied Belgrade to lead the country to secession in 1991, may call on Drnovsek to form a coalition if his Liberal Democrats remain the largest party.
But the People's Party argued that Kucan could turn to the "Slovenian Spring" alliance if they clinch a combined vote of more than 50 percent.

The Liberal Democrats were unlikely to turn to the leftist United List, who have been opposed to the planned tough economic measures, such as cuts in public spending, to prepare Slovenia for membership of the European Union (EU).
But the People's Party has also expressed reservations over rushing into membership of the EU. Slovenia signed an association agreement with the EU in June and hopes for entry by the year 2001.

Podobnik, whose party is backed largely by farmers, has called for a long transition period on EU entry, with special protection for the agricultural sector, which makes up 20 percent of the Slovenian workforce but accounts for just five percent of national output.
